proof_skeleton_nl: Fix arbitrary integers n, k, l with 0 <= k, l <= n and assume that R(q) := [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q lies in Q[q]. First use Gaussian symmetry to replace k and l by a := min(k, n-k) and b := min(l, n-l), so the quotient becomes [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q with 0 <= a, b <= n/2. A degree comparison shows that a cannot be smaller than b; otherwise the reduced quotient would have negative degree and could not be a polynomial. Now set d := a-b, A := n-a, and B := b. The quotient is then the interval product Q_{A,B,d}(q) = prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)). The central new input is the bottleneck lemma L4: polynomiality of this reduced interval quotient implies the existence of a weighted polynomial ring S = Q[x_1, ..., x_d] with variable weights B+1, ..., B+d and a homogeneous regular sequence of degrees A+1, ..., A+d. By the standard complete-intersection Hilbert-series formula L5, the Hilbert series of S/(f_1, ..., f_d) is exactly the same interval product, hence exactly the original q-binomial quotient. Since positively weighted polynomial rings and their homogeneous quotients have finite-dimensional graded pieces (L7), the Hilbert series lemma L6 shows that every coefficient of this Hilbert series is a nonnegative integer. Therefore the original polynomial quotient has only nonnegative coefficients. Since n, k, and l were arbitrary, this proves the theorem.

steps.derives: Set a := min(k, n-k) and b := min(l, n-l). Then [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q, and 0 <= a <= n/2 and 0 <= b <= n/2.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L1 once with r = k and once with r = l. Replacing each index by its complement does not change the corresponding Gaussian coefficient, so the quotient is unchanged after replacing k by a and l by b. By the definition of minimum, both a and b lie in the interval [0, n/2].

From A1, the original quotient equals [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q and is a polynomial by the theorem hypothesis. If a < b, then A1 gives 0 <= a < b <= n/2, so L2 implies that [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q cannot belong to Q[q]. This contradicts the hypothesis. Therefore a >= b.

steps.derives: Define d := a - b, A := n - a, and B := b. Then d >= 0, A >= B >= 0, and [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q = Q_{A,B,d}(q) := prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)).
steps.trivial_justification: A2 gives d = a-b >= 0. Since A1 gives a <= n/2, we have A = n-a >= a, and A2 gives a >= b = B, hence A >= B >= 0. Now apply L3 to the reduced pair (a,b) to rewrite [n choose a]_q / [n choose b]_q as the displayed interval product. Combining with A1 yields the same formula for the original quotient.
A3 identifies Q_{A,B,d}(q) with the original quotient, and the theorem hypothesis states that the original quotient is a polynomial in q.

steps.derives: Let S := Q[x_1, ..., x_d] be graded by deg(x_i) = B+i. Then there exist homogeneous polynomials f_1, ..., f_d in S such that deg(f_i) = A+i for every i and f_1, ..., f_d is a regular sequence.
steps.trivial_justification: A3 provides the parameter bounds A >= B >= 0 and d >= 0, and A4 provides the polynomiality of Q_{A,B,d}(q). Therefore the hypotheses of L4 are satisfied, so L4 yields the required homogeneous regular sequence in the weighted polynomial ring S.

steps.derives: If I := (f_1, ..., f_d), then I is a homogeneous ideal of S and Hilb_{S/I}(q) = prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)) = Q_{A,B,d}(q) = [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q as an identity of formal power series.
steps.trivial_justification: Because the f_i found in A5 are homogeneous, the ideal I they generate is homogeneous. Apply L5 with weights w_i := B+i and degrees e_i := A+i. This gives Hilb_{S/I}(q) = prod_{i=1}^d (1 - q^(A+i)) / (1 - q^(B+i)). By A3, that same product is exactly Q_{A,B,d}(q), and A3 also identified Q_{A,B,d}(q) with the original q-binomial quotient.

steps.derives: For every integer m >= 0, the homogeneous component (S/I)_m is finite-dimensional over Q.
steps.trivial_justification: The grading weights of S are B+1, ..., B+d, all of which are positive. A6 states that I is a homogeneous ideal of S. Therefore L7 applies and gives finite-dimensionality of every graded piece of the quotient ring S/I.

steps.derives: The formal power series [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q has coefficients in Z_{>=0}; since it is polynomial by hypothesis, that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.
steps.trivial_justification: By A7, the graded Q-vector space S/I has finite-dimensional homogeneous pieces, so L6 applies to M := S/I and shows that Hilb_{S/I}(q) has nonnegative integer coefficients. A6 identifies Hilb_{S/I}(q) with [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q. Hence the coefficients of the quotient are all nonnegative; because the theorem hypothesis already says the quotient is a polynomial, this is exactly the desired coefficientwise nonnegativity.

steps.derives: For all integers n, k, l with 0 <= k, l <= n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose l]_q is a polynomial in q, then that polynomial has only nonnegative coefficients.
steps.trivial_justification: The argument from A1 through A8 was carried out for arbitrary integers n, k, l satisfying 0 <= k, l <= n under the sole additional hypothesis that the quotient is a polynomial. Therefore universal generalization yields exactly the root theorem.
